title: Pricing questions in a minute
objectives: Answer quick risk-neutral pricing questions: a forward, a digital, a power payoff.

screens.prose: Drill, two minutes. Say the reason first: price is the discounted $Q$-expectation. Our market: $S_0 = 100$, $r = 5\%$, $\sigma = 20\%$, $T = 1$. The curve is $S_T$ under $Q$ (drift $r$), with $S_T > 100$ shaded. A digital call pays £1 if $S_T > 100$.
screens.question: What is the digital call's price today? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: The label shows the shaded chance under $Q$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the shaded chance off the curve, then discount it from time $T$.

byKey.no-discount: You gave the $Q$-chance 0.5596 as a price. £1 arrives at time $T$, so we discount by $e^{-rT} = 0.9512$.
byKey.real-drift: You used the real drift 12%, so $\Phi(0.5) = 0.6915$, then discounted. Prices use the $Q$ drift $r$, not $\mu$.
byKey.coin: You called it a fair coin. The curve is skewed up: $Q(S_T > 100) = \Phi(d_2)$ ${}= 0.5596$.

explain.text: The shaded chance is $\Phi(d_2) = \Phi(0.15)$ ${}= 0.5596$, and discounting gives £0.5323. The real drift $\mu$ never enters.

screens.prose: Next, a forward struck at 100: it pays $S_T - 100$ at $T$. The payoff is linear, so no model of $S_T$ is needed: $E_Q[S_T] = S_0e^{rT}$ ${}= 105.1271$.
screens.question: What is the forward worth today, in £? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Discount the strike, not the share: $S_0 - Ke^{-rT}$.

byKey.free: You called an at-the-money forward free. It is free only when $K = S_0e^{rT} = 105.1271$.
byKey.forward-price: You gave the forward price $S_0e^{rT}$. The contract's value is today's share less the discounted strike.
byKey.simple: You gave $rS_0 = 5$, simple interest on the share. The strike discounts at $e^{-rT}$: $95.1229$.

explain.text: A forward needs no volatility: $\sigma$ appears nowhere in $S_0 - Ke^{-rT}$. That is why it is the first answer to give.

screens.prose: Now the digital put, which pays £1 if $S_T < 100$. The curve shades that side. Its chance under $Q$ is $\Phi(-d_2) = 0.4404$.
screens.question: What is the digital put's price? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: The shaded chance is on the other side of 100.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Discount the shaded $Q$-chance 0.4404.

byKey.no-discount: You gave the chance 0.4404 without discounting. £1 at time $T$ is worth $e^{-rT}$ times that chance.
byKey.complement: You took $1 - 0.5323 = 0.4677$. The two digitals add to $e^{-rT} = 0.9512$, not to 1.

explain.text: The call and the put together pay £1 for certain, so they must add to the bond, $e^{-rT} = 0.9512$. Say that check aloud: it catches a missing discount at once.

screens.prose: A power payoff pays $S_T^2$ at $T$. Build its price, each line with its reason. Leave out the two flawed lines.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: Normal mgf: $E[e^{aZ}] = e^{a^2/2}$ with $a = 2\sigma\sqrt{T}$ gives the factor $e^{2\sigma^2T}$.

lines.why: The mean of a square exceeds the square of the mean. The gap is $e^{\sigma^2T}$.

lines.text: Use the real drift $\mu$ in $S_T$, since prices should reflect expected growth.
lines.why: A price is a $Q$-expectation. The hedge removed $\mu$, so the drift is $r$.

hints.text: The mgf of $Z$ gives the extra $e^{2\sigma^2T}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write $S_T$ under $Q$, square it, use the mgf, then discount.

byKey.x1: You squared the mean. For a convex payoff that undervalues it by the factor $e^{\sigma^2 T}$.
byKey.x2: You put the real drift in. Replace $\mu$ by $r$ before taking the expectation.
byKey.left-out: A line of the working is in the Left out list. Only the two flawed lines belong there.

explain.text: The extra $e^{\sigma^2T}$ over $(S_0e^{rT})^2$ is the price of convexity: volatility makes a convex payoff worth more.

screens.prose: A junior prices the power claim as "the share squared": $e^{-rT}(S_0e^{rT})^2$. Another leaves out the discount. Use the line you just built, with $S_0 = 100$, $r = 5\%$, $\sigma = 20\%$ and $T = 1$.
screens.question: What is the claim's price in £? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Price $= S_0^2e^{(r + \sigma^2)T}$. Compute $e^{0.09}$.

byKey.jensen: You squared the forward and discounted: $10^4e^{0.05} = 10{,}512.71$. That misses the factor $e^{\sigma^2T}$.
byKey.spot: You gave $S_0^2 = 10{,}000$, today's share squared. The claim pays at $T$, after growth and convexity.

explain.text: The convexity term $e^{\sigma^2T} = 1.0408$ lifts the price from £10,512.71 to £10,941.74. Say "the mean of a square is more than the square of the mean".

screens.prose: Any payoff splits into pieces we can price. The call is the asset-or-nothing payoff (the share if $S_T > 100$) less 100 digitals. Take $S_0\Phi(d_1) = 63.6831$ and $\Phi(d_2) = 0.559618$.
screens.question: Price 100 digitals and the call, to 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Price the digital as in screen 1, multiply by 100, then subtract.

byKey.r1c1: One digital is $e^{-rT}\Phi(d_2) = 0.532325$. For 100 of them, $53.2325$. Without discounting you would get 55.96.
byKey.r2c1: The call is $63.6831 - 53.2325 = 10.4506$. A sum, not a difference, would give 116.9.

explain.text: The pieces recover the Black-Scholes price: £10.4506. When a payoff is odd, split it into a share-or-nothing piece and cash digitals.

screens.prose: Edge case. A claim pays £1 at $T$ whatever happens. There is no $S_T$ in it, so no $\sigma$ either.
screens.question: What is it worth today? Give 4 decimal places.

byKey.none: You gave £1, no discounting. Money later is worth less than money now.
byKey.simple: You subtracted $r$, giving 0.95. Continuous discounting is $e^{-rT} = 0.9512$.
byKey.grow: You grew £1 by $e^{rT}$. A future payment is discounted back, not grown.

explain.text: The bond is the unit every other price is built from, and the sum check for digitals: call plus put equals $e^{-rT}$.

screens.prose: The interviewer pushes the question one step: a payoff $S_T^n$ for any $n$. The same line as before, with $2$ replaced by $n$ in the exponent of $S_T$.
screens.question: Give $E_Q[S_T^n]$ in terms of $S_0$, $n$, $r$, $\sigma$ and $T$.

widget.label: E_Q of S_T to the n

hints.text: The mgf gives $E[e^{aZ}] = e^{a^2/2}$ with $a = n\sigma\sqrt{T}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Raise $S_T$ to the $n$ and use the mgf with $a = n\sigma\sqrt{T}$.

byKey.jensen: You gave $(E_Q[S_T])^n$, which ignores the spread of $S_T$. The mgf adds $\tfrac12n^2\sigma^2T$.
byKey.no-var: You left out the mgf factor $e^{n^2\sigma^2T/2}$. It is the effect of the noise on a power.

explain.text: Check $n = 1$: the exponent is $rT$, the forward. Check $n = 2$: it is $(2r + \sigma^2)T$, which matches screen 4. Both checks take seconds.

screens.prose: Make the five-minute answers executable. Each formula uses `math.erf` for $\Phi$, and `mc_price` checks any payoff by simulation on 1,000,000 draws of seed 16.
screens.question: Complete the four functions.

tests.call: [round(v, 4) for v in mc_price(lambda s: s ** 2, 100, 0.05, 0.2, 1, 1000000, 16)]
[round(v, 4) for v in mc_price(lambda s: np.maximum(s - 100, 0), 100, 0.05, 0.2, 1, 100000, 11)]

widget.how: Submit runs 8 hidden tests: the forward, digitals at two strikes, powers (including n = 1, 3 and 0.5), and two simulations on seeds 16 and 11, with a three-standard-error check against the formula.

hints.text: Simulate $S_T$ under $Q$, discount each payoff and take mean and standard error.

feedback.correct: The formula gives £10,941.74 for $S_T^2$; seed 16 simulates £10,948.77 with standard error £4.56, within 1.6 standard errors.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the examples: the forward is 4.8771 and the digital call 0.5323.

explain.text: A one-minute formula and a simulation that agrees give two independent checks. Quote the formula; keep the simulation for your own reassurance.

screens.prose: A desk quant is asked to price a digital call and digital put at 100 on the spot. A junior writes 0.5323 and 0.4677: "they add to 1." You say: "They must add to the bond, $e^{-rT}$, and 0.5323 plus 0.4677 does not."
screens.question: By how much does the junior's pair miss the sum that must hold? Give 4 decimal places.

widget.accept: The sum must be $e^{-0.05} = 0.9512$; the junior's pair sums to 1, so it is off by $1 - 0.9512 = 0.0488$.
widget.label: Miss

hints.text: The pair together pays £1 for certain at $T$.

feedback.correct: $1 - 0.9512 = 0.0488$: the junior forgot to discount the put.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the pair's sum with the bond $e^{-rT}$.

byKey.none: You accepted a sum of 1. The two digitals pay £1 at $T$, so they are worth the bond, not £1.
byKey.bond: You gave the required sum 0.9512, not the miss. The miss is the gap between that and the pair's sum.
byKey.simple: You gave $r = 0.05$ as the miss. Continuous discounting makes it $1 - e^{-0.05} = 0.0488$.

explain.text: Habit: after any digital, add the call and put and compare with $e^{-rT}$. The junior's pair is £0.0488 per £1 too dear, £48.80 on £1,000 of notional.

ideas: Price is $e^{-rT}E_Q[\text{payoff}]$: drift $r$, never $\mu$, and always discount.
A forward is $S_0 - Ke^{-rT}$ with no $\sigma$. A digital call is $e^{-rT}\Phi(d_2)$, and call plus put equals the bond $e^{-rT}$.
For a power, $E_Q[S_T^n]$ ${}= S_0^n\exp\!\big(n(r$ ${}- \tfrac12\sigma^2)T$ ${}+ \tfrac12n^2\sigma^2T\big)$, and the mean of a square exceeds the square of the mean.

formula.name: Power payoff
formula.note: At $n = 1$ this is the forward $S_0e^{rT}$. Discount by $e^{-rT}$ for the price.

summary.trap: Do not square the forward: $E[S_T^2] \neq (E[S_T])^2$, and do not skip the discount.

quiz.question: What is the forward price of the share for delivery in 2 years ($S_0 = 100$, $r = 5\%$)? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Grow continuously: $S_0e^{rT}$ with $T = 2$.

byKey.simple: You used simple interest, $100(1 + 0.05 \times 2) = 110$. Continuous growth compounds.
byKey.one-year: You gave the one-year forward. The delivery is in two years.

explain.text: Continuous compounding over two years multiplies by $e^{0.1} = 1.10517$.

quiz.question: A claim pays $\ln S_T$ at $T = 1$ (our market). What is its price? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the mean of $\ln S_T$ under $Q$, then discount.

byKey.no-discount: You gave the $Q$-mean 4.6352 without discounting it.
byKey.no-drift: You discounted $\ln 100 = 4.6052$ and dropped the drift $r - \tfrac12\sigma^2 = 0.03$.

explain.text: $\ln S_T$ is normal under $Q$ with mean $\ln S_0 + (r$ ${}- \tfrac12\sigma^2)T$, so no integral is needed.

quiz.prose: Four claims on our share, all at $T = 1$.
quiz.question: Which price does not depend on $\sigma$?

options.why: You forgot that $d_2$ holds $\sigma$. The digital depends on volatility through $\Phi(d_2)$.
You forgot the mgf factor $e^{\sigma^2T}$. The square depends on $\sigma$.
You forgot that an option's price rises with volatility. It depends on $\sigma$.

feedback.correct: A linear payoff needs only $E_Q[S_T]$, which is free of $\sigma$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which payoff is linear in $S_T$?

explain.text: $E_Q[S_T] = S_0e^{rT}$ has no $\sigma$, so the forward needs none. Every nonlinear payoff does.

quiz.question: What is the price of a claim paying $S_T^3$ (our market)? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The exponent is $-r + n(r - \tfrac12\sigma^2)$ ${}+ \tfrac12n^2\sigma^2$ at $n = 3$.

byKey.jensen: You cubed the forward and discounted: $10^6e^{0.10}$ ${}= 1{,}105{,}170.92$. That misses the convexity factor.

explain.text: The exponent is $-0.05 + 3 \times 0.03$ ${}+ \tfrac12 \times 9 \times 0.04$ ${}= 0.22$. Cubes pay a larger convexity premium than squares.
